course.title: How the Body Works
course.description: How the body's main systems work and how they fit together, from cells and tissues to the heart, lungs, gut, kidneys, nerves, hormones and the immune system. Each lesson pairs a mechanism with a practical health link, such as what a blood pressure reading means or how a vaccine works, and none of it is personal medical advice.
course.audience: A curious adult with no biology since school who wants to understand what their own body is doing and to read health information with confidence. They need everyday arithmetic and nothing else. The course does not diagnose, treat or advise any individual, and it does not replace a conversation with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist.

paragraphs: How the body's main systems work and how they fit together, from cells and tissues to the heart, lungs, gut, kidneys, nerves, hormones and the immune system. Each lesson pairs a mechanism with a practical health link, such as what a blood pressure reading means or how a vaccine works, and none of it is personal medical advice.
outcomes: You'll be able to name the four basic tissues and say how one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell.
You'll be able to explain homeostasis and trace a negative feedback loop for temperature and for blood pressure.
You'll be able to follow blood through the heart and calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume.
You'll be able to read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic and say why one reading is not a diagnosis.
You'll be able to explain how air moves in and out, how oxygen reaches the blood, and how to read a respiratory rate against the normal ranges.
You'll be able to follow food through the alimentary canal and work out an energy budget and the WHO's sugar and salt limits.
introduction.prerequisites: No earlier Discere course is needed.

modules.title: Building blocks and balance
modules.description: Cells, tissues, the idea of a steady internal state, and the bones and muscles that show how use shapes tissue.

modules.title: Circulation, breathing and digestion
modules.description: How blood is pumped and measured, how air and food are taken in, and how oxygen and nutrients reach the blood.

modules.title: Energy, balance and control
modules.description: How food becomes energy, how the kidneys, nerves and hormones keep the body steady, and how the immune system and vaccines protect it.

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.summary: Early, unspecialised cells become specialised in structure and function as the body develops from a single fertilised egg.

concepts.title: Tissue
concepts.summary: Cells of one kind or a few kinds organised into layers that do one job; the body has four broad categories: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.

concepts.title: Stem cell
concepts.summary: An unspecialised cell that can divide without limit as needed and can, under specific conditions, differentiate into specialised cells.

concepts.title: Cell cycle control
concepts.summary: Internal and external stop and advance signals decide when a cell divides; loss of that control can lead to cancer.

concepts.title: Homeostasis
concepts.summary: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life.

concepts.title: Negative feedback
concepts.summary: A response that opposes the change that set it off, so a value is held within a narrow range.

concepts.title: Positive feedback
concepts.summary: A response that adds to the change that set it off, as with oxytocin and labour contractions.

concepts.title: Baroreceptor reflex
concepts.summary: Stretch receptors report blood pressure to the cardiovascular centre, which adjusts the heart and vessels to bring it back.

concepts.title: Bone remodelling
concepts.summary: Osteoblasts form new bone while osteoclasts break down old bone, and the balance between them constantly reshapes it.

concepts.title: Osteoporosis
concepts.summary: A decrease in bone mass that occurs when the rate of bone resorption exceeds the rate of bone formation.

concepts.title: Muscle contraction
concepts.summary: In skeletal and cardiac muscle, myosin pulls on actin once calcium ions expose binding sites, and the process needs ATP.

concepts.title: Hypertrophy and atrophy
concepts.summary: More sarcomeres and myofibrils in each fibre with training, or fewer with disuse; the number of fibres does not change.

concepts.title: Relative risk
concepts.summary: A statement such as a 20 to 30 percent increased risk compares one group with another and is not a count of deaths.

concepts.title: Four chambers
concepts.summary: Two upper receiving chambers, the atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the ventricles, one pair on each side.

concepts.title: Pulmonary and systemic circuits
concepts.summary: The pulmonary circuit takes blood to and from the lungs; the systemic circuit takes oxygenated blood to the tissues and returns it.

concepts.title: Cardiac output
concepts.summary: The amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute: stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

concepts.title: Resting heart rate
concepts.summary: 60 to 100 beats per minute for a normal adult; below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia.

concepts.title: Blood
concepts.summary: A connective tissue with formed elements (red cells, white cells, platelets) suspended in the fluid plasma.

concepts.title: Arteries, capillaries and veins
concepts.summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries exchange nutrients and wastes, and veins return blood to the heart.

concepts.title: Systolic and diastolic pressure
concepts.summary: The higher number is the pressure when the ventricles contract; the lower is the pressure when they relax.

concepts.title: High blood pressure
concepts.summary: Pressure in the blood vessels that stays too high; it usually causes no symptoms and is found only by measuring.

concepts.title: Respiratory membrane
concepts.summary: The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together, about 0.5 micrometres thick, across which gases pass by simple diffusion.

concepts.title: Pulmonary ventilation
concepts.summary: Movement of air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure differences made by the diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs.

concepts.title: Passive expiration
concepts.summary: Normal breathing out needs no muscular energy; the lungs recoil as the muscles relax.

concepts.title: Respiratory rate
concepts.summary: Breaths per minute; 12 to 18 for an adolescent or adult, and higher in young children.

concepts.title: Alimentary canal
concepts.summary: A one-way tube from the mouth to the anus, modified as the pharynx, esophagus, stomach and the small and large intestines.

concepts.title: Propulsion and peristalsis
concepts.summary: Swallowing is voluntary; peristalsis is the involuntary sequence of alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that moves food along and mixes it.

concepts.title: Absorption
concepts.summary: Broken-down nutrients pass from the canal into the bloodstream or, for lipids, into lacteals, mainly in the small intestine.

concepts.title: Folds, villi and microvilli
concepts.summary: Three features of the lining that increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine more than 600-fold.

concepts.title: Lactase
concepts.summary: The enzyme that digests the milk sugar lactose; too little of it leads to lactose intolerance.

concepts.title: ATP from glucose
concepts.summary: Glucose from digested carbohydrate is taken up by cells in response to insulin and broken down by glycolysis to make ATP.

concepts.title: Basal metabolic rate
concepts.summary: The daily energy used at rest; about 70 percent of daily expenditure goes to basic organ functions, 20 percent to physical activity and 10 percent to temperature control.

concepts.title: Nutritional Calorie
concepts.summary: The heat needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 degree Celsius, which differs from the physics calorie.

concepts.title: Four principles of a healthy diet
concepts.summary: Adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity (WHO).

concepts.title: Nephron
concepts.summary: One of about a million tiny structures in each kidney that filter the blood, removing wastes and extra water as urine.

concepts.title: Glomerular filtration rate
concepts.summary: The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute; about 125 mL a minute in males and 105 mL in females, which is about 180 and 150 litres a day.

concepts.title: Reabsorption
concepts.summary: About 99 percent of the filtrate returns to the circulation, leaving 1 to 2 litres of urine a day.

concepts.title: ADH and aquaporins
concepts.summary: ADH inserts water channels in the collecting ducts; more ADH gives more concentrated urine and less gives dilute urine.

concepts.title: Other kidney jobs
concepts.summary: Regulating pH, helping control blood pressure, making most of the body's erythropoietin and finishing the activation of vitamin D.

concepts.title: Action potential
concepts.summary: A brief electrical signal in which the membrane potential rises from about -70 mV, reaches about +30 mV and returns.

concepts.title: Chemical synapse
concepts.summary: A neurotransmitter released from one cell crosses a small gap and binds to receptors on the next cell.

concepts.title: Sensory receptor and transduction
concepts.summary: Specialised receptor cells change the stimulus into a change in membrane potential.

concepts.title: Reflex arc
concepts.summary: Sensory input, central processing at a synapse in the spinal cord, and motor output, as in withdrawing a hand from a hot stove.

concepts.title: Demyelination
concepts.summary: Loss of the insulation around axons, as in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system.

concepts.title: Hormone and target cell
concepts.summary: A hormone travels in the blood but affects only cells with receptors for it.

concepts.title: Insulin and glucagon
concepts.summary: Insulin, from beta cells, lowers blood glucose; glucagon, from alpha cells, raises it; each is switched off as the level moves back.

concepts.title: Type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: Cells become resistant to insulin, the pancreas makes more, and over time the beta cells become exhausted.

concepts.title: Early signs of diabetes
concepts.summary: Excessive urination and thirst, because glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine.

concepts.title: Prevention of type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: WHO lists a healthy body weight, at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week, a healthy diet that avoids sugar and saturated fat, and not smoking.

concepts.title: Innate and adaptive responses
concepts.summary: The innate response is rapid but nonspecific; the adaptive response is slower at a first infection but highly specific and effective.

concepts.title: Antibody and antigen
concepts.summary: An antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds a specific antigen, a structure on the surface of a pathogen.

concepts.title: Immunological memory
concepts.summary: On re-exposure the secondary response is stronger and faster, often clearing the pathogen before any symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccine
concepts.summary: A killed or weakened pathogen, or its components, that builds immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccination coverage
concepts.summary: The share of a group that has received doses; WHO reports it by vaccine and year.

lessons.title: Cells and tissues
lessons.orientation: Name the four basic tissue types, say how one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell, and explain why a failure of the controls on cell division matters for health.

lessons.title: Keeping the body steady
lessons.orientation: Explain homeostasis as a dynamic balance kept by feedback, trace a negative feedback loop for body temperature and for blood pressure, and tell negative from positive feedback.

lessons.title: Bones and muscles
lessons.orientation: Describe how bone is constantly rebuilt and how muscle contracts using ATP, and say what use and disuse do to each, with the WHO's physical activity figure read correctly.

lessons.title: The heart
lessons.orientation: Follow blood through the four chambers and the two circuits, calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume, and say what exercise does to heart rate and output.

lessons.title: Blood vessels and blood pressure
lessons.orientation: Put the vessels in order along the path of blood, read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic, and describe how clinics and home checks use thresholds without treating one reading as a diagnosis.

lessons.title: Lungs and breathing
lessons.orientation: Explain how pressure differences move air in and out, how oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane, and how a respiratory rate is read against the normal ranges.

lessons.title: Digestion
lessons.orientation: Follow food along the alimentary canal, separate propulsion, mixing, chemical digestion and absorption, and explain why the small intestine is where most absorption happens and what lactose intolerance shows about enzymes.

lessons.title: Nutrition and energy
lessons.orientation: Trace how food becomes ATP, read an energy budget split of 70, 20 and 10 percent, and use the WHO's four principles and its sugar and salt limits to judge a day's food, without personal dietary advice.

lessons.title: Kidneys and water balance
lessons.orientation: Describe filtration and reabsorption in the nephron, use the 180 litres a day and 99 percent figures to find the daily urine volume, and explain how ADH changes the urine.

lessons.title: Nerves and senses
lessons.orientation: Describe an action potential from a described voltage graph, follow a signal across a synapse and through a reflex arc, and say what happens to signalling when myelin is damaged.

lessons.title: Hormones and blood sugar
lessons.orientation: Explain how hormones reach only their target cells, how insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose between 70 and 100 mg/dL, what goes wrong in type 2 diabetes, and what the WHO lists for prevention.

lessons.title: The immune system and vaccines
lessons.orientation: Separate innate from adaptive immunity, explain why a second exposure gives a stronger and faster response, say what a vaccine is, and read vaccination coverage figures.
